Every index = extra structure written on every INSERT. Row goes to table, then each index gets its own entry: B-tree traversal to find the leaf, page write, WAL/redo log record, occasional page split. N indexes → roughly N+1 writes per row.

How much it hurts depends on key order. Monotonic key (autoincrement id, timestamp) → appends to rightmost leaf, cheap, cached. Random key (UUIDv4, hash, email) → each insert hits a random leaf → page splits, cache misses, random I/O once index outgrows RAM. That's usually the cliff: fine until index no longer fits in buffer pool, then inserts fall off.

Other multipliers: unique index → lookup before every insert to check for duplicates; wide/composite/expression keys → bigger entries, more splits; in Postgres, a new index on an updated column also kills HOT updates, so UPDATEs slow too.

Fixes, in order of payoff: drop unused or redundant indexes (Postgres: `pg_stat_user_indexes` where `idx_scan = 0`; MySQL: `sys.schema_unused_indexes`); batch inserts into multi-row statements or one transaction; for bulk loads, drop index → load → recreate (one sorted build beats millions of incremental inserts); swap random keys for time-ordered ones (UUIDv7); use partial index if queries only touch a subset of rows.

Which DB, and what column is the index on? That narrows it to one cause.
